# OneCoin/Cryptoqueen: Evidence-Constrained Reconstruction

**Context date:** October 1, 2026.  
**Evidence base:** This report uses only the two benchmark-returned sources identified as `SRC-001` and `SRC-002`. Details not supported by those sources are omitted. The report distinguishes official enforcement statements, allegations summarized by a secondary source, investigative assessments, and unresolved claims.

## Executive summary

According to the U.S. Department of Justice, OneCoin was an international cryptocurrency investment scheme that operated from 2014 to 2019. It was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, and marketed a cryptocurrency called OneCoin through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. The DOJ identified Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood as co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. and stated that they and others orchestrated the scheme. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The DOJ stated that investors put more than $4 billion into the fraudulent cryptocurrency worldwide. It also reported that more than $40 million in forfeited assets were available for victim compensation as of its April 13, 2026 announcement. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation, while the DOJ’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The available evidence supports the following high-level structure:

- **OneCoin Ltd.** was the identified company, based in Sofia, Bulgaria.
- **Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood** were identified by the DOJ as co-founders.
- **The MLM network** was the documented distribution structure.
- **Greenwood** was described by the secondary source as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and was reported as sentenced to 20 years in prison.
- **Ignatova** remains the subject of an FBI investigative pursuit and is described by the DOJ as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive.
- **Ignatova’s current whereabouts and status are unresolved** in the returned evidence. The sources do not establish whether she is alive, dead, detained, or located.

The returned evidence does **not** establish a complete organizational chart, the identities and roles of all other participants, a full corporate-entity map, German or Bulgarian official findings, or any particular account concerning Ignatova’s disappearance or possible death.

## Scope and evidentiary standards

### Source limitations

Only two benchmark source IDs were returned:

- `SRC-001`: an official U.S. Department of Justice announcement concerning victim compensation and enforcement status.
- `SRC-002`: a secondary legal-industry article summarizing the OneCoin prosecution and Greenwood’s sentence.

`SRC-001` is the stronger source for official enforcement facts, government characterizations, forfeiture, victim compensation, and Ignatova’s wanted status. `SRC-002` is useful for additional details about alleged scheme mechanics and Greenwood’s reported sentence, but it is not itself a judgment, indictment, sentencing memorandum, or other primary court record.

### Classification used in this report

- **Established enforcement fact:** A fact expressly stated by the DOJ or another law-enforcement authority in `SRC-001`.
- **Reported adjudicated outcome:** A conviction or sentence reported by `SRC-002`, where the underlying court record was not returned.
- **Allegation:** A prosecution theory or alleged misrepresentation summarized in `SRC-002`.
- **Enforcement assessment:** A characterization made by the DOJ, FBI, IRS-CI, or a U.S. Attorney.
- **Unresolved or unknown:** A matter for which the returned sources provide no substantiated answer.

## Origin, identity, and chronology of the scheme

### Start and operating period

The DOJ stated that OneCoin began operations in 2014 and that the scheme operated between 2014 and 2019. It described OneCoin as based in Sofia, Bulgaria. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The secondary source similarly described OneCoin as beginning operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and stated that it began operating in the United States around 2015. Because the latter detail is supplied by a secondary source and the returned excerpt does not provide the underlying filing, it should be treated as a reported account rather than an independently established enforcement fact. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Company and product

The DOJ identified **OneCoin Ltd.**, also referred to as **OneCoin**, as the relevant company and stated that it was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. It stated that the company marketed and sold a cryptocurrency “by the same name.” [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The sources do not establish the existence or role of additional OneCoin-related corporations, foundations, payment processors, exchanges, blockchain companies, or subsidiaries. Those entities should not be added to the reconstruction on the present evidence.

## Operating structure

### Global MLM distribution network

The DOJ described OneCoin’s distribution method as a **global multi-level-marketing network**. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The secondary source stated that members received commissions for recruiting other people to purchase cryptocurrency packages. This is presented there as part of the government’s account of the scheme’s operation. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

On the returned evidence, the supported structural description is therefore:

1. OneCoin Ltd. marketed OneCoin as a cryptocurrency.
2. Distribution occurred through a global MLM network.
3. Members were allegedly incentivized through commissions linked to recruitment and package purchases.
4. The scheme attracted investment from victims in multiple countries.

The sources do not provide enough information to identify particular regional leaders, distributors, recruiters, payment channels, or internal departments. No further hierarchy should be inferred.

### Alleged cryptocurrency representations

The secondary source reported that prosecutors alleged two significant misrepresentations:

- OneCoin’s value was represented as being determined by market supply and demand, although prosecutors alleged that its value was set arbitrarily without regard to market forces.
- OneCoin was represented as having a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions, although prosecutors alleged that no publicly verifiable blockchain existed.

These are **allegations summarized by `SRC-002`**, not independently established facts supplied by a returned primary court record. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The DOJ’s broader enforcement characterization was that OneCoin was “a lie disguised as cryptocurrency” and that victims were misled by “falsified statements and empty promises.” Those statements should be understood as official law-enforcement assessments of the scheme. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

## Principal founders and documented roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identified Ruja Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. and stated that she and Greenwood, together with others, orchestrated the international investment scheme. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The returned evidence therefore supports the following description:

- **Entity relationship:** co-founder of OneCoin Ltd.
- **Scheme relationship:** identified by the DOJ as one of the people who orchestrated the scheme.
- **Law-enforcement status:** subject of an ongoing FBI investigative pursuit and described by the DOJ as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive.

The evidence does not supply a complete account of Ignatova’s specific operational duties, financial role, communications, or relationship with every other participant. Such details should not be added without additional source support.

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

The DOJ identified Karl Sebastian Greenwood as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. and as one of the people who orchestrated the scheme with Ignatova and others. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The secondary source described Greenwood as:

- a co-founder of OneCoin;
- OneCoin’s top MLM distributor; and
- a person alleged to have received 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling more than $300 million.

Those financial and distribution details are reported by `SRC-002` as part of the government’s allegations. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

`SRC-002` also reported that Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. Because the returned evidence does not include the underlying judgment or sentencing record, the precise conviction counts, sentencing date, docket details, and complete forfeiture terms cannot be stated here as independently verified court-record facts. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### “Others” involved in the scheme

The DOJ stated that Ignatova and Greenwood acted “with others,” but `SRC-001` does not identify all of those people or describe their roles. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The research materials refer to searches for Mark Scott, Konstantin Ignatov, and Irina Dilkinska, but the returned evidence does not provide substantive, source-supported findings about their roles, relationships, charges, convictions, sentences, or current status. They are therefore omitted from the factual organizational reconstruction.

## Scale, victims, and alleged or documented activities

### Investment and loss figures

The DOJ stated that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The secondary source reported that prosecutors alleged more than $4 billion in investments from approximately 3.5 million investors. The investor count is therefore reported as a prosecution-related figure in the secondary source, not as an independently verified figure from the returned official announcement. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Marketing and recruitment

The supported account is that OneCoin marketed a purported cryptocurrency through an international MLM network. The secondary source reported that the network involved commissions for recruiting purchasers of cryptocurrency packages. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Alleged manipulation of value and transaction records

According to the allegations summarized in `SRC-002`, OneCoin’s value was presented as market-based even though prosecutors alleged that it was set arbitrarily. Prosecutors also alleged that OneCoin claimed to use a private blockchain when no publicly verifiable blockchain existed. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

These details describe the alleged mechanics underlying the prosecution’s fraud theory. The returned material does not include the underlying technical evidence, expert testimony, exhibits, or judicial findings needed to expand on them.

## Enforcement actions and victim recovery

### U.S. prosecutions and investigations

The DOJ stated that it brought a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York and that several key figures had been sentenced. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The DOJ identified the FBI and IRS-CI as the agencies that conducted the criminal fraud investigation. It also stated that the DOJ’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The returned sources do not provide a complete list of prosecutions, defendants, charges, verdicts, sentences, or international cooperation measures.

### Forfeiture and compensation

The DOJ stated that it pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the fraud scheme. It reported that more than $40 million in forfeited assets were available for victim compensation as of its April 13, 2026 announcement. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The same announcement stated that victims who purchased OneCoin between 2014 and 2019 might be eligible for compensation. It identified Kroll Settlement Administration LLC as the remission administrator and stated that the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section managed the remission process. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The announcement stated that the filing deadline was June 30. The returned excerpt does not clearly specify the year in the sentence describing the deadline; because the announcement is dated April 13, 2026, the deadline should not be restated with a year unless the source expressly supports it.

The DOJ also warned that neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice would ask victims to pay to participate in the compensation process. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The approximately $300,000 forfeiture attributed to Greenwood by `SRC-002` should not be assumed to be the source of, or identical to, the more than $40 million available for compensation. The returned sources do not explain the relationship between those amounts. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

## Ruja Ignatova’s current status

### Established enforcement position

The DOJ stated that the FBI continues its investigative pursuit of Ruja Ignatova and described her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive. It asked anyone with information to submit a tip through the FBI. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The secondary source stated that Ignatova remained at large and had been added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### What remains unresolved

The returned evidence does not establish:

- Ignatova’s current location;
- whether she is alive or dead;
- whether she has been detained or located;
- whether any reported disappearance account is accurate;
- whether any alleged death or disappearance theory has been officially confirmed; or
- the outcome of any German or Bulgarian investigation concerning her status.

The research queries sought reporting about possible death, a yacht, and Bulgarian or German proceedings, but no additional source ID supporting those subjects was returned. Those matters must therefore be recorded as **unsupported by the present evidence**, rather than described as established allegations or investigative findings.

The correct evidence-based conclusion as of the contextual date is that Ignatova’s status is unresolved in the returned sources, while U.S. authorities continue to describe her as wanted and subject to investigative pursuit.

## What can and cannot be concluded

### Supported conclusions

The returned evidence supports these conclusions:

1. OneCoin began operations in 2014 and operated through 2019.
2. It was based in Sofia, Bulgaria.
3. OneCoin Ltd. marketed a purported cryptocurrency called OneCoin.
4. Distribution used a global MLM network.
5. Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood were identified by the DOJ as co-founders.
6. The DOJ said they and others orchestrated an international investment fraud.
7. Victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide, according to the DOJ.
8. U.S. authorities investigated and prosecuted OneCoin-related conduct.
9. More than $40 million in forfeited assets were reported as available for compensation in April 2026.
10. Ignatova’s current whereabouts and status remain unresolved in the returned evidence, while the FBI continues to pursue her.

### Unsupported or incomplete matters

The evidence does not support a complete answer concerning:

- all founders or senior participants beyond Ignatova and Greenwood;
- the roles of Mark Scott, Konstantin Ignatov, or Irina Dilkinska;
- all companies or entities connected to OneCoin;
- the complete MLM hierarchy;
- the exact criminal counts and judgments in every prosecution;
- the complete forfeiture structure;
- German or Bulgarian official proceedings;
- the factual basis of claims that Ignatova died, was killed, used a yacht, or remains concealed; or
- a definitive determination of whether Ignatova is alive or dead.

## Conclusion

The publicly documented account supported by the returned evidence describes OneCoin as a Sofia-based, international cryptocurrency investment scheme that began in 2014 and operated through 2019. Its documented distribution structure was a global MLM network. The DOJ identified Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood as co-founders and characterized the scheme as fraudulent, with worldwide victim investment exceeding $4 billion.

Greenwood’s reported 20-year sentence is supported in the returned materials by a secondary legal source, while the DOJ confirms the broader enforcement and compensation context. Ignatova remains the subject of an FBI investigative pursuit and is described as a fugitive. Her present status is not resolved by the available evidence. Any account that goes beyond that conclusion—including claims about her death, location, or concealment—should be omitted unless supported by an additional benchmark-returned source ID.

## Sources

- [SRC-001 — Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)
